Introduction

Starting a Hospice in North Dakota represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals requiring end-of-life palliative and supportive services while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through North Dakota Medicaid and the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

With a significant unmet need, as over 30% of the population lives more than a 30-minute drive from the nearest hospice provider, and Medicaid daily reimbursement rates of $161-$205 per day (in addition to more comprehensive Medicare rates), North Dakota offers a market with significant access gaps and underserved populations, providing a strong opportunity for new providers focused on rural and specialized care. The state’s landscape is ripe for entrepreneurs prepared to navigate the specific licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements of this vital service.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice in North Dakota, from understanding state and federal regulations to building your team, developing referral sources, and preparing for your first inspection.

Table of Contents

  • Understand North Dakota’s Hospice Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand North Dakota’s Hospice Regulations

North Dakota regulates Hospice programs through the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS), which is responsible for overseeing initial licensing, certification, ongoing compliance with state rules, and the overall quality of care for hospice agencies. Because hospice is a federally defined benefit, providers serving Medicare or Medicaid populations must also comply with stringent federal frameworks, primarily the CMS Conditions of Participation (CoPs) and HIPAA.

The regulatory framework emphasizes a philosophy of palliative and supportive services, focusing on patient-centered care, comprehensive pain and symptom management, interdisciplinary team collaboration, and robust protection of patient rights. Compliance involves meticulous documentation, quality oversight through a QAPI program, and adherence to care planning protocols. Licenses in North Dakota typically require renewal every 1 to 3 years, contingent on successful surveys and continued compliance.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While North Dakota issues a single “Hospice Program” license, the services you provide are defined by the four levels of care mandated by Medicare. Each has different staffing, documentation, and reimbursement requirements:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): The most common level of care, provided in the patient’s place of residence, whether that is their private home, an assisted living facility, or a nursing home.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of crisis to manage acute medical symptoms. This involves more intensive nursing care for a minimum of 8 hours in a 24-hour period, primarily provided by nurses and hospice aides.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): For pain or symptom management that cannot be handled in another setting. This care is provided in a Medicare-certified hospital, skilled nursing facility, or dedicated inpatient hospice unit.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term inpatient care provided to the patient to give their primary caregiver a rest. This is limited to five consecutive days at a time.

Program size can range from a small startup agency with a patient census of 10-20 patients to a large regional provider serving over 100 patients. Demand is strongest in rural and frontier areas, regions serving Native American communities, and for specialized services like pediatric hospice. While urban centers have more established providers, less populated regions may offer significant entry opportunities with less competition for agencies prepared to handle the logistics of rural healthcare delivery.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Providers in North Dakota typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC), S-Corporation, C-Corporation, or a non-profit 501(c)(3) entity. Regardless of your chosen structure, you must complete several foundational steps before applying for a license:

  • Register your business with the North Dakota Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a complete licensing application to the NDHHS, including all required documentation, policies, and proof of financial viability.

After state licensure, you must undergo the Medicare certification process, which involves a separate application and a rigorous on-site survey. The entire licensing and certification timeline generally ranges from 6 to 18 months, depending on your team’s readiness, the completeness of your application, and agency survey backlogs.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is essential for securing funding and guiding your launch. Startup costs for a hospice agency in North Dakota typically range from $200,000 to $1,000,000. This covers licensing fees, legal and consulting costs, office setup, initial payroll, and operating capital to cover expenses before reimbursement begins.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by your clinical and administrative team, with staffing representing 60-70% of total costs. Your financial projections should be based on realistic revenue assumptions.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges include:

  • Annual Revenue: Projections can range from $500,000 to $5,000,000+ depending on patient census and service mix.
  • Medicaid: North Dakota Medicaid offers a daily rate of approximately $161 to $205.
  • Medicare: The primary payer, with four tiered daily rates corresponding to the levels of care (RHC, CHC, GIP, Respite). These rates are significantly higher than Medicaid and are adjusted annually by geographic location.

Due to the high costs of care and regulated reimbursement rates, hospice is a mission-driven, low-margin business. Providers operating at an average daily census of 85% or higher of their projected capacity generally achieve net margins below 5%. Reaching break-even can take 18 to 24 months.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

While most hospice care is delivered in the patient’s home, your agency requires a physical office that serves as your administrative hub. This location must be compliant with local zoning and state requirements.

Key facility requirements for a hospice office include:

  • An administrative area for staff to work and collaborate.
  • A secure, locked area for storing patient records to ensure HIPAA compliance.
  • A conference or training room for Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) meetings and staff education.
  • Accessibility for individuals with disabilities (ADA compliance).
  • Sufficient parking for staff.

If you plan to offer General Inpatient (GIP) care in your own facility, it must meet much stricter healthcare facility standards, including life safety codes, patient room requirements, nursing stations, and family common areas. Location selection should consider proximity to referral sources like hospitals and skilled nursing facilities, as well as the ability to attract a qualified workforce.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

The foundation of any successful hospice is its Interdisciplinary Group (IDG), a team of professionals who work together to create and manage each patient’s plan of care. CMS mandates that this team include specific roles.

Required roles for a North Dakota hospice typically include:

  • Medical Director: A physician who provides clinical oversight and direction for the IDG.
  • Registered Nurse (RN) Case Manager: Manages the patient’s clinical care, coordinates visits, and supervises hospice aides.
  • Medical Social Worker (MSW): Addresses the patient’s and family’s psychosocial needs, provides counseling, and connects them with community resources.
  • Spiritual or Pastoral Counselor: Offers spiritual support consistent with the patient’s and family’s beliefs.
  • Hospice Aides (CNAs): Provide personal care to the patient under the supervision of an RN.
  • Volunteer Coordinator & Volunteers: Manages a required volunteer program that provides companionship and respite for families.

All staff must receive comprehensive orientation on the hospice philosophy, pain and symptom management, patient rights, infection control, and the agency’s policies and procedures. Ongoing continuing education is also mandated to ensure the team remains current on best practices.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

To achieve licensure in North Dakota and certification from CMS, you must develop a comprehensive set of written policies and procedures that govern every aspect of your operation. These documents are the blueprint for compliance and quality care.

North Dakota requires written policies covering, at a minimum:

  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Patient Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Functions and Documentation
  • Initial and Comprehensive Patient Assessments
  • Volunteer Program Management
  • Bereavement Program Services
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI)
  • Infection Control and Emergency Preparedness

Individualized care plans are the cornerstone of hospice. They must be developed by the IDG in collaboration with the patient and family, reviewed at least every 15 days, and meticulously documented to reflect the patient’s changing needs and goals.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike many businesses, hospice marketing is not focused on direct-to-consumer advertising. Instead, success depends on building strong, trust-based relationships with professional referral sources who interact with patients and families facing end-of-life decisions.

Referrals for hospice care in North Dakota typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Oncology centers and other specialist physicians
  • Skilled nursing facilities (SNFs)
  • Primary care physicians and clinics, especially in rural areas
  • Assisted living facility administrators and nurses

Your marketing efforts should focus on demonstrating your agency’s value proposition: exceptional clinical care, responsiveness to referrals, excellent communication with partners, and strong compliance. Successful providers are known for their reliability and the quality of their outcomes, which becomes their most powerful marketing tool.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight of your hospice agency is ongoing. You will be subject to periodic, unannounced inspections (surveys) from NDHHS and CMS surveyors. If you choose to become accredited, you will also have reviews from your accrediting organization, such as The Joint Commission or CHAP.

Inspections are focused on ensuring you are following your own policies and meeting all state and federal regulations. Common deficiencies cited during hospice surveys often relate to:

  • Incomplete or inconsistent documentation in the plan of care.
  • Failure to update the patient’s medication list.
  • Lack of comprehensive IDG meeting documentation.
  • Issues with hospice aide supervision and care planning.
  • Deficiencies in the Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program.

To ensure you are always ready for a survey, you must foster a culture of continuous quality improvement. This involves conducting regular internal audits, staying current on regulatory changes, and maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

  • How long does it take to open a Hospice in North Dakota?

The entire process, from business planning to accepting your first patient, can take 12 to 24 months. This includes time for business registration, policy development, state licensing, Medicare certification, and staff hiring and training.

  • What licenses are required?

You need a Hospice Program license from the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS). Critically, to receive reimbursement from the vast majority of payers, you must also achieve Medicare certification through CMS, which involves a separate application and survey process.

  • What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement primarily comes from the Medicare Hospice Benefit, which pays a per diem rate based on one of four levels of care. North Dakota Medicaid also provides a daily rate of approximately $161-$205. Some private insurance plans also offer a hospice benefit, but Medicare remains the dominant payer.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice in North Dakota is a challenging yet deeply rewarding venture. The clear need for expanded access, particularly in rural and underserved communities, creates a powerful opportunity for mission-driven entrepreneurs. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of the complex regulatory environment, and an unwavering commitment to operational discipline.

Providers who invest in robust compliance systems, hire and train a compassionate and qualified team, and build strong relationships with community referral partners are best positioned for long-term sustainability and success in serving the people of North Dakota.
